look_here_first: Introduced invasive warm-season Kleberg bluestem. Start at the 2–15 thin upright/fingerlike paired-spikelet racemes and examine a RING of conspicuous WHITE HAIRS at stem nodes, which is especially useful in this species. Magnify sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets, the awn and lower glume; a hairy pinkish head alone is not species proof.
photo_note: Temporary one-photo learner coverage. Keep until stronger diagnostic gallery coverage replaces or supplements it. 2026-10-21: photograph visually inspected; Original photo visibly shows an erect bundle of slender pigmented seed-bearing branches and long fine awns. It cannot resolve the diagnostic WHITE RING at the vegetative stem node, which lies off-frame. Field comparison added with 3 visible-structure arrows; no unverified macro features claimed.
identification_caution: Photographed in New South Wales, Australia; this is an introduced/management comparison grass, NOT a Hays native planting recommendation.

best_field_traits: Often sprawling or creeping via stolonlike lower shoots and eventually ascending erect to about 1 m.
A prominent node collar of WHITE HAIRS is a signature feature; must be photographed at node, not assumed from panicle.
Inflorescence of 2–15 fingerlike racemes bearing paired sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets.
Spikelets often silvery or purplish, with hairy axes and awned fertile florets; numbers vary.
Introduced/invasive management grass, NOT native restoration seed.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Actual stem node WHITE ring hairs and creeping stolon/rootstock
One sessile awned vs one pedicelled companion spikelet at mm scale
Whole rooted clump with multiple culm nodes
crew_field_check: Start from whole rooted plant to establish growth form.
Photograph flowering head and collar on same individual.
Use hand-lens/25x macro to measure floret structure when needed; photos without it support only provisional source determination.
No county native certification; Kew states D. annulatum and D. sericeum are introduced in Texas.

comparisons.key_distinctions: D. sericeum is an introduced silky bluestem also with very hairy silvery flowering branches, but often tufted with shorter rhizomes rather than distinctly stoloniferous. D. annulatum is strongly associated with unmistakable white-ringed stem nodes, and its full flowering head may bear more subdigitate racemes. Distinguish both from Bothriochloa/Schizachyrium with paired-spikelet + glume macro; photo of a red-purple foxtail alone is insufficient.
